quarterly_data.signal: Q2 2026 segment and P&L detail (CFO Susan Li): Family of Apps revenue was $60.4 billion, up 28% year over year, and Family of Apps ad revenue $59.4 billion, up 27% (26% in constant currency). Impression growth was healthy across all regions, driven by engagement and user growth and ad load optimizations; the average price per ad rose on ad performance gains, better macro conditions than in Q2 2025 and currency tailwinds, partly offset by strong impression growth from lower-monetizing surfaces and regions. Reality Labs revenue was $431 million, up 16%, on strong growth in AI glasses revenue, partly offset by lower Quest headset sales. Q2 total expenses were $42 billion, including the $2.4 billion legal charge and $1.2 billion of severance for the May 2026 headcount reduction; besides third-party AI token and cloud costs, expense growth came from employee compensation (technical hires, particularly AI talent), higher depreciation and data center operating costs, and legal-related costs. Operating income was $18.8 billion, an 8% decline year over year and a 31% operating margin; excluding the legal charges and severance it would have increased 9%. Tax rate 16%; net income $15.8 billion, or $6.18 per share. Meta ended Q2 with over 75,000 employees, down 3% from Q1, a total that includes approximately 8,000 employees impacted by the May 2026 reduction, the majority of whom Meta expects to be out of the headcount by the end of Q3 2026.
quarterly_data.figure: Family of Apps revenue $60.4 billion (up 28%); Family of Apps ad revenue $59.4 billion (up 27%); Reality Labs revenue $431 million (up 16%); operating income $18.8 billion (31% operating margin); EPS $6.18

quarterly_data.signal: Outlook details (CFO Susan Li): the Q3 2026 revenue guidance assumes foreign currency is an approximately 1% headwind to year-over-year total revenue growth, based on current exchange rates. Meta continues to monitor active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact its business and results, including scrutiny on youth-related issues in several markets and a number of youth-related trials scheduled this year in the U.S., which 'may ultimately result in a material loss'.
quarterly_data.figure: approximately 1% foreign-currency headwind to Q3 2026 year-over-year revenue growth

quarterly_data.signal: Engagement and recommendations (CFO Susan Li): Instagram global time spent grew double digits year over year, largely from feed and Reels recommendation improvements; Facebook video time spent rose 9% globally and over 10% in the U.S. and Canada on ranking improvements. Meta shipped its largest single-release Reels ranking improvement to date (faster inference plus a new architecture drawing on deeper user history), which drove a 15 basis point increase in Instagram sessions; it is now being brought to Feed, where early results look comparable. This quarter Meta began using its Muse family of models for content understanding (video topic classification and summarization) with positive early results. Instagram's Your Algo page lets users tune recommendations with natural-language prompts, and Facebook's Shape Your Feed shows over 80% retention among users who engage with it. Next-generation work includes foundation models designed to power organic content and ads recommendations simultaneously, and LLM-native recommender systems. In the Q&A she said Meta sees 'further headroom to continue improving recommendations over the rest of the year and into 2027' and grew the number of launches from its ranking agents this half. CEO Mark Zuckerberg: the new Muse Image and Muse Video models 'will also dramatically expand the universe of content that people can discover across our platforms'.
quarterly_data.figure: Facebook video time spent up 9% globally; 15 basis point increase in Instagram sessions; over 80% retention for Shape Your Feed

quarterly_data.signal: Ads monetization (CFO Susan Li): in Q2 Meta completed its global ads expansion on Threads; on WhatsApp it introduced support for more ad destinations and advertiser performance goals in Status and continues on track toward the global rollout. Early pilots using LLMs to better understand user preferences drove a 1% increase in app event conversions on Instagram. Meta introduced a new end-to-end creative solution that translates advertisers' real performance signals into their next creative decision, built with agency integrations from day one, and with the rollout of Muse Image it expects to further expand advertisers' ability to generate high-quality, on-brand creatives at scale.
quarterly_data.figure: 1% increase in app event conversions on Instagram from early LLM pilots

quarterly_data.signal: Business agents and enterprise (CEO Mark Zuckerberg): Meta business agents became available globally this quarter on WhatsApp and Messenger and are now rolling out on Instagram; Meta is building agentic features that summarize customer conversations and surface what customers ask for, later suggesting ways to grow the business and competitive intelligence, aiming over time at a 'business-in-a-box' service. Monetization is a mix of subscriptions and volume-based pricing, and he expects more of these products to evolve to be 'like our ad systems, where businesses only pay us when we achieve results for them'. Meta One, the new subscription offering, will get a variety of tiers and pricing options as demand grows. Beyond marketers, Meta built coding and internal productivity tools for its own use and sees a large opportunity to serve small and larger businesses with them, 'a somewhat different muscle than we have historically had'; he frames the enterprise opportunity as the sum of compute sales, API services, productivity services and business agents beyond marketing, 'a very, very large opportunity', and Meta expects 'to grow a large business serving large customers'.

Models and API (CEO Mark Zuckerberg, CFO Susan Li): in the last month Meta Superintelligence Labs shipped Muse Spark 1.1 and Muse Image; the CEO said Muse Spark 1.1 'excels at computer use, tool use, and multimodal understanding' and that Meta is ramping up distribution through partner channels and more coding agents over the coming weeks. CFO: Meta launched a 'high-intelligence model API at a competitive price' and is encouraged by the initial results; it soon expects to roll the model API out to more distribution channels, make it available in more countries and open it up for enterprises. In the Q&A the CEO said Meta is 'in the process of scaling much larger and more advanced models', while simpler, more efficient models will serve the vast majority of consumer prompts; open-weight models are no substitute because 'Right now, the open-source models are not as strong as the frontier models', and Meta, which has 'built our own data centers, our own infrastructure, our own chips, our own low-level software', sees 'sovereignty over building your own models' as an important part of that stack.

Personal agents and consumer apps (CEO Mark Zuckerberg): Meta is developing personal agents that 'can work 24/7 on your behalf' as the foundation for its next wave of products and revenue lines; he called it 'extremely unlikely' that five years out billions of people will not have such an agent, said consumer agents must 'just work', unlike today's proto-agents that take a lot of fiddling, and on timing: 'we're going to ship this at some point soon' and 'We haven't done that yet'. WhatsApp is already the leading surface where people engage with Meta AI; this quarter Meta launched incognito mode on WhatsApp and the Meta AI app for private conversations with the assistant 'that even Meta can't see'. Product velocity: Instagram Instants shipped earlier this year, and Meta just launched Forum, a standalone groups app, and Seller, a standalone marketplace app; 'I expect it to become a lot easier to ship new apps'.

Compute supply and allocation (CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Q&A): 'there's just nowhere near enough compute for all the demand', which is why Meta receives a large number of offers for its compute while it has many valuable internal uses, and Meta is itself also buying compute; 'it would be foolish to basically just sell all of the compute and take a short-term profit' when intelligence built on top compounds its value, so Meta uses a lot of its capital to build out compute, confident it can monetize compute directly when that makes sense. A substantial amount of Meta's compute goes to training models 'to be a leading lab'; the rest spans the core business, new consumer products, the API, business agents, developer tools and direct compute sales, where he expects 'meaningful growth in all of these areas'. Data centers being built now come online only after a lead time. CFO Susan Li: longer term, 'the supply chains need to be built out to support the capacity that we anticipate we and others will need'; she cited 'the uncertainty over long-term constraints on building capacity' as one of the two factors behind focusing on 2026 and 2027 capacity; past incremental capacity 'has proven extremely valuable in scaling experiences like Reels', and 'being on the frontier will unlock new markets and opportunities for which we may need additional compute'.

AI glasses (CEO Mark Zuckerberg): 'Our glasses remain one of the fastest-growing consumer electronics of all time.' Meta just released its own line of Meta glasses in collaboration with EssilorLuxottica, including a style designed with Kylie Jenner; they are the first glasses to ship with Muse Spark out of the box, and 'Early sales have been strong, exceeding our expectations'.
